questions.prompt: A 24 V supply drives a motor at 25 % duty. Average voltage in volts.
A servo uses 1 ms for 0 degrees and 2 ms for 180 degrees. Angle for a 1.4 ms pulse, in degrees. Precision 0.5.
A 1.8 degree stepper is driven at 1/8 microstepping. Microsteps per revolution.
A 200 step per revolution stepper at 1/16 microstepping drives a 2 mm-lead screw at 15 mm/s. Step pulses per second.
Same motor (0.3 A no load, 5.5 A stall, 0.9 N m stall torque, 12 V). Current in amperes at a 0.45 N m load.
A 12 V motor (200 rpm no load, 0.9 N m stall torque) runs at 80 % duty from a 12 V supply with a 0.3 N m load. Speed in rpm. Precision 0.5.
For the same motor and supply, what duty (fraction) gives 100 rpm at a 0.15 N m load? Precision 0.005.
A motor is loaded at 0.2 N m. Compared with 100 % duty, how many rpm does the load take away at 50 % duty?
options: Half as many, since the duty is halved.
Twice as many, since the motor is weaker at low duty.
The same number: the droop does not depend on duty.
None, because PWM removes the effect of the load.
questions.explanation: Loaded speed is w_nl x V/V_rated - w_nl x torque / stall torque; the second term does not contain the duty.

questions.prompt: In a home-built H-bridge, Q1 (high side, left) and Q3 (low side, left) are both switched on. What happens?
options: The supply is shorted to ground through one leg.
The motor brakes by shorting its own terminals.
The motor reverses its direction of rotation.
Nothing: the motor sees zero volts and just coasts.
questions.explanation: Two switches on the same leg connect the supply directly to ground (shoot-through); real driver chips add dead time to prevent it.

questions.prompt: A robot-arm joint must report position, load and temperature over a shared serial bus. Which type fits?
options: A hobby servo driven with 1 to 2 ms pulses.
A stepper with a STEP and DIR driver.
A brushed DC motor with an H-bridge.
A smart serial servo with digital packets.
questions.explanation: Smart serial servos exchange digital packets and report position, load and temperature; hobby servos give no readback.

questions.prompt: A servo twitches whenever the wheel motors start, and both share one 5 V rail. Most likely cause and fix?
options: The pulse is too long: shorten it to 1 ms and retry.
The rail sags in surges: give the servo its own supply, common ground.
The servo is stalled: raise the PWM frequency to 20 kHz.
The pulses are in microseconds: switch them to milliseconds.
questions.explanation: Motor current surges pull the shared rail down and disturb the servo and logic; separate rails with a common ground fix it.

questions.prompt: A stepper runs fine at 200 steps/s but loses position at 6000 steps/s with a load. Best first remedy?
options: Remove the load and trust the step count anyway.
Increase the PWM frequency of the supply to 20 kHz.
Choose a larger microstep size and ignore the step rate.
Ramp the speed up and lower the top speed.
questions.explanation: Pull-out torque falls with speed. Ramping, a lower top speed or more voltage keeps the rotor in step; open-loop steppers cannot report lost steps.

questions.prompt: A small brushed motor whines loudly at low speed from an Arduino Uno's default analogWrite. What is the usual cause?
options: The PWM frequency, a few hundred hertz, is audible.
The duty cycle is above 100 % at low speed.
The H-bridge is in the coast state during the off time.
The motor voltage is above the 36 V driver limit.
questions.explanation: The Uno default is about 490 Hz for most pins, which is audible; about 20 kHz is inaudible but costs more switching loss.

questions.prompt: A 12 V motor stalls at 5.5 A; the driver is rated 1.7 A continuous and 2.5 A peak. What is the right conclusion?
options: Safe: the running current is below the 1.7 A continuous rating.
Safe: the peak rating applies to the whole run, not just seconds.
Unsafe in a jam: add a current limit and stall detection.
Unsafe only if the PWM frequency is below 1 kHz or so.
questions.explanation: Stall current above the peak rating means a blocked wheel can overheat or trip the driver; limit, detect or oversize.

questions.prompt: Write a test plan for a function driver_check(i_needed, i_stall, i_cont, i_peak) that returns overload, stall-exceeds-peak, stall-short-only or ok.
rubric: Hand-computes one case for each of the four outputs.
Tests boundaries: running current exactly at the continuous rating and stall exactly at the peak rating.
Checks the priority order when several conditions are true, and invalid inputs such as negative current.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Choose a motor type and a driver for a 1 kg two-wheel robot and justify it against two alternatives.
rubric: Picks a type from the job (for example a brushed gearmotor with an encoder) and states the torque requirement.
Compares at least two alternatives (stepper, BLDC, smart servo) on feedback, efficiency, cost and complexity.
Lists the driver numbers checked: voltage range, continuous current and stall current against the peak rating.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A robot resets whenever both wheels start moving. Give a diagnosis plan: what you would measure, the likely causes and the fixes.
rubric: Measures the supply voltage during start-up with a scope or a logging multimeter and the motor current.
Names inrush or stall current sagging the rail (brown-out) and a shared logic and motor supply as causes.
Proposes fixes: separate rails with common ground, bulk capacitor, soft start or current limit, and re-test.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
